channel.title: Open Source on Agent Memory: AI Memory Systems Explained
channel.description: Recent content in Open Source on Agent Memory: AI Memory Systems Explained

item.title: LangMem vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick LangMem if your agent already runs on LangGraph and you want memory tools inside that graph, saved to a LangGraph store you run. Pick Hindsight if you want memory as its own server, shared by several agents or frameworks, with published benchmark scores and a reflect operation.

LangMem and Hindsight solve the same problem in different places. LangMem is code you import into a LangGraph app. Hindsight is a service your agents call over its API, an MCP server or a plugin. Facts about LangMem come from its README and repository, read 28 November 2026. Facts about Hindsight come from its README, its benchmarks site and its pricing page.

item.title: MemOS vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick MemOS if you want an Apache 2.0 memory system with a graph and a local SQLite plugin for Hermes Agent or OpenClaw, and you are fine running Neo4j and Qdrant for the server. Pick Hindsight if you want one MIT server that you can run on Postgres alone, or use as a hosted API, and you want the published BEAM 1M and 10M scores.

Both projects are open source and both are run by the companies that sell them. MemOS is made by MemTensor. Hindsight is made by Vectorize. Facts about MemOS come from its README and repository, read 28 November 2026. Facts about Hindsight come from its README, its benchmarks site and its pricing page.

item.title: Cognee vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick Hindsight if you want the whole memory server under MIT, a reasoning call (reflect) and a published BEAM 1M score. Pick Cognee if your agent needs to remember documents, code and business tools such as Slack, Notion, Linear and Google Drive, and you want a knowledge graph built from them.

The two solve different parts of the problem. Cognee starts from content and turns it into a graph you can search. Hindsight starts from what the agent learns and keeps it as facts, observations and mental models. Hindsight facts come from its README, benchmarks site and pricing page. Cognee facts come from its README, its BEAM report, its pricing page and its GitHub license, all read on 27 November 2026.

item.title: Graphiti vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick Hindsight if you want a finished memory server under MIT that you can run with one Docker command, with no graph database to run beside it. Pick Graphiti if you are building a temporal knowledge graph into your own system and you want to control the graph database, the prompts and the service yourself.

Graphiti is a library, not a service. Its author says it is “self-hosted only” and that you “operate the graph database, retrieval, and surrounding service yourself”. Hindsight is a memory server you run or use as a hosted API. Graphiti facts come from its README and repository (github.com/getzep/graphiti, read 27 November 2026). Hindsight facts come from its README, benchmarks site and pricing page.

item.title: Honcho vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description: Short answer: pick Hindsight if you want the whole memory server under MIT, or if your histories are long and you want its published BEAM results. Pick Honcho if you want memory that models each user, agent or group as a peer, or if median answer speed matters more to you than cost. In the one head-to-head run we found, the two were close on accuracy, Hindsight was cheaper, and Honcho was faster than Hindsight.

item.title: Hindsight vs Supermemory: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick Hindsight if you want the whole memory server open source and self-hosted, or long histories with a published lead on BEAM. Pick Supermemory if you want memory, document search and Google Drive or Gmail connectors behind one hosted API, and you do not want to run infrastructure.

Both are real options. Neither vendor’s numbers are independent, so this page gives the source of each figure. Hindsight facts come from the Hindsight README, its benchmarks site and its pricing page. Supermemory facts come from its README, its self-hosting and pricing pages and its LongMemEval report, all read on 26 November 2026.

item.title: Letta vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick Letta if you want a complete agent to run: its own memory, tools, terminal and chat channels, ready to use. Pick Hindsight if you already have an agent, framework or coding tool, and you want a memory server to plug into it.

Letta and Hindsight solve different parts of the same job. Letta builds the agent around memory. Hindsight is one memory layer that many agents share. Facts for Letta come from its README, its pricing page, its blog and its benchmark post, read on 26 November 2026. Hindsight facts come from its README, benchmarks site and pricing page.

item.title: Zep vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared (November 2026)
item.description:
Short answer: pick Hindsight if you want the whole memory server open source and running on your own machine or cloud, or if your histories are long and you want the published BEAM lead. Pick Zep if you want a managed context platform with connectors to business apps, and you are happy to pay for it.

For the open-source framework alone, without Zep’s managed service, see Graphiti vs Hindsight.

The two projects differ more than their feature lists suggest. Zep sells a managed service with a graph under it. Hindsight is a memory server you run or use as a hosted API. Hindsight facts come from its README, its benchmarks site and its pricing page. Zep facts come from its research and pricing pages, its memory benchmark page and the Graphiti and Zep repositories, all read on 26 November 2026.

item.title: OpenViking (2026): What It Is, Setup and Memory
item.description: OpenViking is an open-source context database for AI agents from the Viking team at ByteDance’s Volcengine. It keeps everything an agent knows (documents, long-term memories and skills) in one virtual filesystem under viking://, writes a short summary for every directory, and lets agents read context with file commands like ls, tree, find and grep. Memories come from sessions: when a chat is committed, OpenViking extracts them in the background as Markdown files you can open and edit.

item.title: Mnemosyne vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Compared
item.description:
Mnemosyne vs Hindsight is a choice between a small local library and a full memory server. Mnemosyne is one pip install and one SQLite file, built first for Hermes Agent, and runs on a Raspberry Pi. Hindsight runs as a server on PostgreSQL, searches four ways at once, and consolidates facts into observations it can reason over with reflect.

On benchmarks, Mnemosyne’s own README puts Hindsight ahead: 73.4% to 65.2% on BEAM at 100K, with a judge-model caveat. Mnemosyne publishes no end-to-end score on longer histories, where Hindsight reports 73.9 at 1M and 64.1 at 10M tokens. This page compares the two on storage, recall, setup, benchmarks and limits, from each project’s README and docs, checked on 20 October 2026.

item.title: agentmemory: Persistent Memory for AI Coding Agents
item.description:
agentmemory is an open-source memory server that gives AI coding agents persistent memory across sessions. Hooks in Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Hermes, OpenClaw and other agents record what the agent does, and the server injects the most relevant past context when the next session starts. You install it with npx -y @agentmemory/agentmemory@latest.

The project lives at github.com/rohitg00/agentmemory, is written in TypeScript under the Apache 2.0 license, and had about 29,900 GitHub stars on 26 October 2026 (29,300 on 12 October). This page covers what it does, how it works, how to set it up, what its benchmark numbers mean, and how it compares with Hindsight and Mem0 for coding-agent memory. Facts come from the agentmemory README and benchmark files, checked on 12 October 2026. (This site, aiagentmemory.org, has no connection to the agentmemory project.)

item.title: TencentDB Agent Memory (v2.0.3): Layers, Team Memory, Setup
item.description:
TencentDB Agent Memory (repo TencentDB-Agent-Memory) is an open-source memory hub for AI agents from Tencent Cloud Database. It sits as a proxy between a coding agent and its LLM, saves each conversation, distills it into four layers (L0 to L3), and injects the right memory, skills, docs and code knowledge into every request. Its Team Memory release lets several agents and people share those assets with access control.

It is MIT-licensed, written mostly in TypeScript, and had about 30,080 GitHub stars on 29 October 2026, up from 29,600 on 19 October. This page covers how its memory layers work, how to install it, what Team Memory adds, which agents it supports, and how it compares with Hindsight and Mem0. Facts come from the project’s README, INSTALL.md, CHANGELOG.md, the GitHub releases list and the SDK README, rechecked on 19 October 2026; the 2.0.3 section comes from the v2.0.3 release notes, read on 29 October 2026.

item.title: Mem0 vs MemPalace: Extracted Facts vs Verbatim Recall
item.description:
Mem0 vs MemPalace is a choice between keeping facts and keeping everything. Mem0 sends each conversation to an LLM, pulls out short facts like “prefers Go,” and returns the matching ones on search. MemPalace saves conversations and files word for word on your machine and finds them later with local search, with no LLM and no API key.

Both are open source and among the most-starred memory projects on GitHub. They solve different problems: Mem0 is a memory layer for apps with many users, MemPalace is a personal, local archive built mostly for coding agents. Hindsight, an MIT memory server, covers ground from both: per-user banks for apps, native plugins for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, a fully local mode, and the top answer-accuracy scores of the three on LongMemEval and BEAM. Facts below come from each project’s README, docs and PyPI page, checked on 12 October 2026.

item.title: Mem0 vs Supermemory: Agent Memory APIs Compared
item.description:
Mem0 vs Supermemory is a choice between a memory-only layer and a memory-plus-context API. Mem0 extracts short facts from conversations and returns them by hybrid search, and you can run all of it yourself. Supermemory does fact extraction too, but bundles it with user profiles, document RAG and data connectors behind one hosted API.

Both have a free tier (since 26 October 2026 Mem0’s needs your own LLM key after 30 days, and its paid plans are custom; Supermemory’s paid plans start at $19/month), and both can run on your machine, though in very different ways. Many teams comparing the two also look at Hindsight, an MIT-licensed memory server that scores highest of the three on LongMemEval and leads Mem0 by 9.8 and 15.5 points on the long-history BEAM 1M and 10M tests. This page compares all three on memory model, retrieval, self-hosting, benchmarks and pricing, using each project’s README, docs and pricing pages and Mem0’s own comparison pages, checked on 12 October 2026. For a side-by-side of Hindsight and Supermemory alone, see Hindsight vs Supermemory.

item.title: Mem0 vs Hindsight: Agent Memory Layers Compared
item.description:
Mem0 vs Hindsight is a choice between two memory layers that sit beside your agent, not inside it. Hindsight does more work per memory: it links entities and time, merges facts into observations in the background, and can reason over them with reflect. Mem0 keeps memory lean: one LLM pass extracts facts, and search returns a small set of them cheaply.

The data splits along that line. On Mem0’s own comparison page, Hindsight leads by 9.8 points on BEAM 1M and 15.5 points on BEAM 10M, the long-history tests, and ships graph, temporal recall and consolidation in its MIT release, where Mem0 keeps them on its paid Platform. Mem0 returns about 4x fewer tokens per retrieval and lists SOC 2 and HIPAA for its Platform. This page compares them on memory model, retrieval, what’s free versus paid, benchmarks and cost, using each project’s README, docs and pricing pages, checked on 12 October 2026. For Supermemory, the third option most teams compare, see Hindsight vs Supermemory.

item.title: Hindsight AI Memory: How It Works and When to Use It
item.description:
Hindsight is an open-source agent memory server from Vectorize, released under the MIT license with the full server included. It gives an AI agent three operations: retain (store and extract facts), recall (search memories) and reflect (reason over them to answer a question). It runs on PostgreSQL with pgvector, self-hosted or as the managed Hindsight Cloud.

Its strongest case is long histories: on the BEAM benchmark it scores 73.9 at 1M tokens and 64.1 at 10M, 9.8 and 15.5 points ahead of Mem0 by Mem0’s own comparison page. It also ships every feature (graph, temporal recall, consolidation, mental models, reflect) in the open-source release. This page covers how it works, what the benchmarks show, its real limits, and when another tool is the better pick. Facts come from the GitHub README, the official docs and the paper, checked on 12 October 2026.

item.title: Letta Alternatives: 7 Agent Memory Options Compared
item.description:
Letta alternatives are memory systems you can use instead of Letta (formerly MemGPT) to give agents long-term memory. The main ones are Mem0, Zep, Graphiti, Cognee, LangMem, Hindsight and Supermemory. Most teams switch because they want a memory layer for their own agent, while Letta is now a full agent runtime that owns the loop.

This page covers what Letta does today, the common reasons to look elsewhere, a comparison table, a short section per option, and how to choose. For a deeper look at Letta itself, see the Letta guide.

item.title: Supermemory Alternatives: 7 Agent Memory Tools Compared
item.description:
Supermemory alternatives are other memory layers for AI agents: Hindsight, Mem0, Zep, Graphiti, Letta, Cognee and Honcho. People usually look for one when they need fully open-source, self-run infrastructure (Supermemory’s local server is a closed-source binary), want memory without bundled RAG and connectors, or need a different memory model such as a temporal graph or an agent that manages its own memory.

Below: what Supermemory does, a comparison table, a short section on each alternative, and how to pick. Facts come from each project’s README, docs and pricing page, checked on 8 October 2026. For Hindsight against Supermemory alone, with the benchmark sources, see Hindsight vs Supermemory.

item.title: Zep Alternatives: Open-Source and Hosted Options
item.description: Zep alternatives are other ways to give AI agents long-term memory: Graphiti (Zep’s own open-source core), Hindsight, Mem0, Letta, Cognee and Supermemory. Most people searching for one want a self-hosted, open-source option, because Zep stopped maintaining its Community Edition in 2025 and is now a managed, credit-priced service. Graphiti is the closest match to Zep’s model; Hindsight is the most complete open-source memory server, with graph and time-range recall, consolidation and reflect all in its MIT release.

item.title: What Is Mem0? How the Mem0 Memory Layer Works
item.description:
Mem0 (“mem-zero”) is an open-source memory layer for AI agents. It uses an LLM to pull durable facts out of conversations, stores them with embeddings per user, agent or session, and returns the relevant ones when you search. It ships as a Python and Node library, a self-hosted Docker server, and the managed Mem0 Platform.

This page explains how Mem0 works today, what changed in the April 2026 release, and how to configure, query and delete memories. Facts come from the Mem0 GitHub README, the Mem0 docs and the pricing page, checked on 8 October 2026; pricing rechecked on 30 October 2026 after Mem0’s 26 October change.

item.title: Best Open-Source Agent Memory on GitHub (2026): Stars, Licenses
item.description:
The leading open-source AI agent memory systems on GitHub are Mem0, MemPalace, Hindsight, Graphiti, Cognee, Letta, LangMem, MemOS, Memori, Honcho, Basic Memory and Memobase. Most are Apache-2.0 or MIT, written in Python, and self-hostable with Docker. They differ in storage (vectors, graphs, files), in how much is truly open versus paid, and in what they’re built for.

If you want the most complete fully open option, it’s Hindsight: its MIT server includes graph and temporal recall, consolidation and reflect, which Mem0 keeps on its paid Platform, and it leads Mem0 on the long-history BEAM benchmark by 9.8 points at 1M tokens and 15.5 at 10M (vendor-run). This page covers only open-source projects: repos, licenses, stars, languages and strengths. Star counts, licenses and last-push dates come from the GitHub API on 26 October 2026, with the change since our 18 October sweep. For hosted options and benchmarks, see the LLM memory comparison. For background, see AI agent memory explained.

item.title: Mem0 Alternatives: 7 Agent Memory Tools Compared
item.description:
Mem0 alternatives are other memory layers that give AI agents long-term memory: Zep, Graphiti, Letta, Cognee, Hindsight, Supermemory and LangMem. Teams usually look for one when they need self-hosted graph memory (removed from open-source Mem0 in v3), temporal facts, an agent that edits its own memory, or different pricing.

For long histories, Hindsight has the strongest published numbers. Mem0’s own comparison page puts it 9.8 points ahead of Mem0 Platform on BEAM at 1M tokens and 15.5 points ahead at 10M, with the two level on LongMemEval.
